title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); the guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (planned episodes = 480). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical shared candidates that passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked and the paired contrast is degenerate. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, an evidence‑based diagnosis of the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into correct device configurations remains a core NetOps challenge. Modern large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed multi‑step configuration sequences from natural‑language intents, but token‑level measures fail to capture operational correctness properties such as command ordering, invariants (e.g., never take both redundant links down), and transient safety constraints. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where a generated configuration is applied within an emulator or device image and deterministically scored—reveals semantic failure modes that text‑only evaluations miss [1].

A frequently proposed mitigation is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline: an LLM generates a candidate; a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants; if the verifier flags violations an automated repair routine attempts a corrected candidate. Prior work documents this pattern across configuration repair and program repair domains and reports improvements for many syntactic and some semantic classes of faults [2,3]. However, important empirical questions remain about how to measure verifier benefit rigorously under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and how evaluation semantics (notably whether paired arms share the same initial generation) affect the estimand and inferential power.

We preregistered a paired experiment to estimate a single, clearly defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline), where unsafe_apply indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused in both arms. This manuscript (1) presents the preregistered design and artifact‑grounded execution accounting, (2) reports confirmatory analysis outputs, and (3) diagnoses why the paired contrast was degenerate in this run and provides artifact‑grounded recommendations for future studies that seek informative paired contrasts.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks surface workflow and planning faults for agentic systems that text‑only tests overlook; NetConfArena is a recent example of this approach [1]. Generate–validate and iterative repair mechanisms are well studied in configuration repair and program repair literature; prototypes demonstrate high repair coverage on certain classes of injected faults but highlight dependence on verifier coverage and repair search strategy [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising directions for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,5]. Engineering precedents such as Batfish document the value of incremental and model‑based verification for network configurations [6].

Our study differs by combining three elements that affect causal interpretation: (a) a preregistered paired estimand, (b) shared_initial_candidate execution semantics that deterministically pair generator output across arms, and (c) closed‑loop deterministic scoring with archived per‑call traces and validator outputs. These choices make the causal role of the verifier explicit: under shared_initial_candidate semantics the verifier can only influence the paired contrast when the single shared candidate fails validation and triggers repair.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate where unsafe_apply = 1 for configurations that would cause a semantic safety violation). The analysis plan specified an exact two‑sided McNemar test for discordant pairs and a 95% bootstrap percentile CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed = 1729) for the paired difference.

Design and sampling: We used a paired design with N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks, blocked into topology/vendor clusters. Task composition followed the preregistered plan: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Tasks were generated deterministically from a task generator that encodes initial states, required command sequences, and per‑task safety constraints. The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and both arms used that same generation; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair per task.

Model, verifier, and scoring contract: Execution declared a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic validator implementing semantic invariants for the emulation environment. Final outcomes are binary: safe (no semantic safety violation when applied) or unsafe (would cause a violation). The verifier records parsed command counts, touched fields, and explicit violation codes; the analysis code maps verifier outcomes to the binary outcome required for the estimand. Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged as potential verifier/simulator inconsistencies and infra failures after allowed retries; exclusion rules and sensitivity analyses were applied as prespecified.

Execution and reproducibility: The preregistered adapter constrained model calls (shared_initial_generation = 1 per task) and repair attempts (≤1 per guarded task). All runtime artifacts (task manifests, per‑call model traces, verifier traces, and analysis CSVs) were archived to permit deterministic reconciliation of the reported numerical outputs to archived artifacts. The preregistration and analysis logs contain the exact bootstrap parameters and seeds used for inference.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: The run completed according to plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240, and model calls consistent with exactly one shared initial generation per task. For the primary binary outcome every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline successes = 240/240 and guarded successes = 240/240. The paired contingency table is n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in the guarded arm because the shared initial candidates passed the deterministic verifier checks in every task. In other words, the single shared generation per task was valid under the verifier and therefore the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to alter the final configuration relative to the baseline. Consequently, repair attempts = 0 across the experiment and all subgroup slices (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial) are degenerate with zero unsafe applies in both arms.

Interpretation of null paired contrast: The observed null difference is an artifact of the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with universal verifier PASS outcomes; under the registered contract the guarded arm can change a paired outcome only if the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation and a repair is applied. Because that did not occur, the experiment correctly and transparently reports an estimate of zero with zero uncertainty under the chosen estimand and execution semantics. This outcome is not evidence that verifiers are useless in principle; rather it shows that the preregistered combination of paired semantics and generator/verifier behavior produced no informative discordant pairs.
sections.discussion:
Design implications and recommendations: The result highlights a tension between (a) conserving model‑call budgets and ensuring direct pairing via a single shared generation and (b) creating opportunities for the verifier and repair mechanism to demonstrate causal effect. To produce informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations we recommend at least one of the following, chosen to align with the causal estimand of interest: (1) independent initial generations per arm so the generator is an active component of the intervention; (2) intentional generator perturbations or increased stochasticity (more samples/temperature settings) to increase the chance of initial candidate failures; (3) larger repair budgets (multiple iterative repairs) so that the repair mechanism can be exercised when validation fails; or (4) stronger or adaptive adversary protocols that increase the frequency of generator failures requiring repair. Each option trades off model‑call costs, experimental complexity, and interpretability of the causal contrast.

Threats to validity: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate semantics was a deliberate preregistered choice that constrains causal interpretation; our artifacts document adherence to that contract. Construct validity: deterministic verifier coverage is finite and may not capture all semantic fault classes; verifier PASS does not guarantee absence of undiscovered semantic risks beyond the verifier's rule set. External validity: tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus and deterministic task generator—extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments and human operator workflows requires careful validation. Conclusion validity: realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 eliminates the ability to detect verifier benefit in this design; future power planning should account for generator variability and adversary strength to ensure nondegenerate discordant-pair counts.

Operational implications: Practitioners designing GVR pipelines should (a) clarify the causal question (verifier as a check on a fixed generator vs. verifier plus repair as an active intervention), (b) select execution semantics consistent with that question (shared vs independent generation), and (c) instrument repair prompts and repair traces to study repair search behavior when repairs occur. Our artifact archive, which contains the full preregistration, per‑task manifests, and verifier outputs, supports reproducible reanalysis and method refinement.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate result is explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with universal verifier PASS outcomes: because a single shared initial candidate per task passed validation in every case, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the guarded arm could not create discordant pairs. We provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for future experiments that seek informative paired contrasts (allow independent generation, increase repair budget, or strengthen adversaries) and document threats to validity and operational implications. The preregistration, per‑call traces, verifier outputs, and analysis artifacts are archived to permit deterministic reconciliation of the reported numbers to the run artifacts.

limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a fixed, preregistered adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier encodes a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
